challenges.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
challenges.prompt: You are given `prices`, where `prices[i]` is a stock's price on day `i`. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell. Return the largest profit you can make, or `0` if no trade makes money.

examples.explain: Buy on day 1 at 1 and sell on day 4 at 6.
Prices only fall, so do not trade.

hints: For a fixed sell day, which buy day is best?
Keep the lowest price seen so far as you scan from left to right.
On each day, the best profit from selling today is price - lowest. Track the maximum.

solution.python:
def max_profit(prices):
    lowest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best

challenges.explanation: The best buy day for any sell day is the cheapest earlier day, so one pass keeps the running minimum and the best price - minimum. Updating the minimum before computing the profit is safe: it only adds a same-day profit of 0.

challenges.title: Longest Substring Without Repeats
challenges.pattern: Variable window with a hash map
challenges.prompt: Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest substring (a contiguous run of characters) in which no character appears more than once. Spaces and symbols count as characters.

examples.explain: "abc" is the longest run with no repeats.

hints: Use a window s[left..right] that never contains a repeat, and grow it one character at a time.
When the new character is already in the window, move left forward until it is not.
Faster: remember each character's last index and jump left to max(left, last + 1) in one step.
challenges.explanation: The window holds no repeats. When the new character was last seen inside the window, left jumps just past that position; max stops left from moving backward when the last sighting is already outside the window (as in "abba"). Every step records the current window length.

complexity.space: O(m), where m is the number of distinct characters

challenges.title: Maximum Sum of k Consecutive Items
challenges.prompt: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the largest sum of any `k` consecutive items. Values may be negative.
hints: Recomputing every window from scratch is O(n k). Neighboring windows share k - 1 items.
Sum the first k items, then slide: add nums[right] and subtract nums[right - k].
Start the best value from the first window's sum, not 0, because all the sums might be negative.

solution.python:
def max_window_sum(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[right] - nums[right - k]
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

challenges.explanation: Build the first window, then slide it one step at a time, adding the entering item and subtracting the one that leaves. Starting best at the first window's sum handles all-negative input.

challenges.title: Shortest Subarray Reaching a Sum
challenges.prompt: Given a positive integer `target` and an array of positive integers `nums`, return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least `target`. If no such subarray exists, return `0`.

examples.explain: The whole array only sums to 8.

hints: All numbers are positive, so growing a window raises its sum and shrinking lowers it.
Grow the window on the right. As soon as the sum reaches the target, try shrinking it from the left.
Record the length inside a while loop that shrinks as long as the window stays valid.

solution.python:
def min_subarray_len(target, nums):
    left = 0
    window = 0
    best = float("inf")
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        window += x
        while window >= target:
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            window -= nums[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best

challenges.explanation: A shortest-valid window: grow until the sum reaches the target, then record and shrink while it stays valid, since each shrink is a shorter valid window. Each index enters and leaves once, so the nested loop is O(n) overall. Positivity is what makes the rule monotonic.

challenges.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
challenges.prompt:
You are given a string `s` of uppercase English letters and an integer `k`. You may change at most `k` characters of `s` into any other uppercase letter.

Return the length of the longest substring that can be made of one repeated letter after those changes.

examples.explain: Change the B in "AABA" to get "AAAA".

hints: To make a window one letter, keep its most frequent letter and change the rest.
So a window needs (length - count of its most frequent letter) changes, and it is valid when that is at most k.
Grow on the right, update the counts, shrink from the left while invalid, and record the length after shrinking.
challenges.explanation: A window needs length - max count changes, so it is valid when that is at most k. This is a longest-valid window: grow, shrink while invalid, then record. Finding the max count scans at most 26 letters, so the total is O(26 n). Keeping a never-decreasing max count avoids the scan, but the simple version is clearer.

complexity.time: O(n), with a factor of up to 26 for the max count

challenges.title: Minimum Window Substring
challenges.pattern: Variable window with a "still missing" counter
challenges.prompt:
Given strings `s` and `t`, return the shortest contiguous substring of `s` that contains every character of `t`, counting repeats: if `t` has two `a`s, the window needs at least two `a`s. Letters are case-sensitive.

If no window works, return the empty string. If several shortest windows exist, return the one that starts first. Aim for O(len(s) + len(t)).

examples.explain: "ba" and "ab" are both length 2; "ba" starts first.
t needs two a characters but s has only one.

constraints: s and t contain English letters
hints: Grow the window by moving `right`. Once it contains everything in `t`, shrink it from `left` for as long as it stays valid, recording each valid window.
Keep a count of how many of each character you still need, plus one number `missing`: how many characters of `t` the window does not cover yet. The window is valid when `missing == 0`.
When a character enters, it reduces `missing` only if it was still needed (its count was above 0). When a character leaves, it increases `missing` only if its count goes back above 0.
challenges.explanation: The right pointer adds characters until the window covers t; the left pointer then removes characters while the window stays valid, so every right end is paired with its shortest valid window. need[ch] going negative records surplus copies, and the single missing counter makes the validity check O(1) instead of comparing two maps. Each pointer moves at most len(s) times. Updating only on a strictly shorter window keeps the earliest of several shortest windows.
